Question_text: A student measures the focal length of a converging lens. The student sets up the apparatus as shown in Fig. 1.1.
image: A diagram shows a converging lens setup on an optical bench. An illuminated object is placed at one end, followed by a stand holding the converging lens, and then a screen at the other end. A metre rule runs along the length of the setup from the illuminated object to the screen.

Parts.part_text: The distance D between the illuminated object and the screen is fixed initially at 1.00 m. The image on the screen is blurred. Describe the adjustment that the student makes to obtain a sharply focused image, without changing D.
The focused image is at the top of the screen. Describe one adjustment that the student makes to move the focused image to the centre of the screen.
The lens is in a holder on a stand. The position of the centre of the lens is to be marked accurately on the stand. Describe how the student does this.

The student finds that, for the same value of D, there are two positions of the lens that produce a focused image on the screen. These positions are at distances u₁ and u₂ from the illuminated object, as shown in Fig. 1.2. The two distances u₁ and u₂ are measured for D = 1.00 m. The values obtained are u₁ = 0.42m and u₂ = 0.56m.
Parts.image: A diagram illustrating the setup with an illuminated object, a converging lens, and a screen. The distance from the object to the screen is labeled 'D'. Two possible lens positions are shown. 'u1' is the distance from the object to the first lens position, and 'u2' is the distance from the object to the second lens position. 'd' is the distance between the two lens positions. The lens is depicted as a double-convex shape with dashed lines showing its other possible position.

Parts.part_text: Calculate the distance d between the two lens positions.
Theory shows that the focal length f of the lens is given by the relationship f = (D² – d²) / 4D. Calculate f.
The student repeats the experiment for different values of D and calculates values of (D² – d²) each time. Fig. 1.3 shows the student's results.
Parts.image: A table titled 'Fig. 1.3' with two columns: 'D/m' and '(D² – d²)/m²'. The rows contain data points: (1.10, 1.08), (1.20, 1.18), (1.30, 1.29), (1.40, 1.38), (1.50, 1.47).

Parts.part_text: On Fig. 1.4, plot the graph of (D² – d²)/m² on the y-axis against D/m on the x-axis. Start your graph from (D² – d²) = 0.90m² and D = 1.00m. Draw the straight line of best fit.
Parts.image: A large grid for plotting a graph. The x-axis is labeled 'D/m' starting from 1.0, and the y-axis is labeled '(D² – d²)/m²' starting from 0.9. The grid is approximately 25x30 large squares, each containing 5x5 smaller squares.

Parts.part_text: Determine the gradient of the line of best fit. Show your working clearly.
Calculate f using the relationship f = gradient / 4.
Explain why it is better to determine f using the method in (c) rather than the method in (b).

Question_text: A teacher demonstrates the force on a wire carrying a current in a magnetic field. Fig. 2.1 shows some of the apparatus used.
image: A diagram showing a magnet with a North (N) pole and a South (S) pole. A wire is positioned horizontally between the poles of the magnet. An arrow on the wire indicates the direction of current flow. The magnet appears to be a U-shaped or block magnet, with the wire passing through the air gap.

Parts.part_text: The current is to be varied and measured. On Fig. 2.1, draw the circuit diagram of the circuit used to provide the current. Include a method to vary and measure the current.
Describe how to increase the current in the wire.
Describe how to reverse the direction of the current in the wire.
Describe how to reverse the direction of the magnetic field.
The current is increased to a very large value. Suggest one problem this may cause.

Question_text: A teacher demonstrates convection in water to a class. The teacher fills a large beaker with cold water, as shown in Fig. 3.1a, and leaves it to stand for 10 minutes. He then places a purple crystal at the bottom of the beaker. The crystal starts to dissolve and the water around the crystal turns purple. Gentle heating is applied to the beaker directly underneath the crystal, as shown in Fig. 3.1b.
image: Two diagrams. Fig. 3.1a shows a large beaker filled with water. Fig. 3.1b shows the same beaker with water, but now a purple crystal is at the bottom and gentle heating is applied directly underneath the crystal. The purple crystal is shown as a small square at the bottom of the beaker.

Parts.part_text: Suggest a reason why the teacher uses a large beaker.
Explain why the teacher leaves the beaker of water to stand for 10 minutes before placing the crystal at the bottom.
Explain why the water is heated gently.
On Fig. 3.1b, draw the initial movement of the water as it is heated gently.
The teacher repeats the demonstration five minutes later. Suggest why it is better to use another beaker of water than to reuse the same beaker and water.

Question_text: A teacher demonstrates the existence of background radiation. Fig. 4.1 shows a counter and a radiation detector placed on a bench, with no laboratory source of radiation present.
image: A diagram showing a counter device connected to a radiation detector. Both are placed on a bench. The counter is a rectangular box, and the detector is a cylindrical probe extending from it.

Parts.part_text: State the name of a suitable detector.
The teacher measures the count for 2 minutes and repeats this five times. The counts recorded each time are: 58, 46, 69, 53, 42
Calculate the average count per second. Give your answer to two significant figures.
State why the five counts are all different.
Explain why safety precautions for radiation hazards are not necessary while taking these readings.
